title: Consume-on-read: destructive DRAM read becomes free reclaim
idea: Add an RD-CONSUME memory command that reverses DRAM's read-then-restore order: the sense amp delivers the line, skips the restore, and the controller flips the line to 'free' in a bitmap. Queues, NN activations and NIC ring buffers that are read exactly once get their capacity back at read time, with no software free or zeroing.
why: Turns fact 8 (destructive read) into a feature: buffer and activation pools shrink ~20-40% because slots recycle at read time, and each consumed read skips the restore part of activate energy.

title: Predictive-coding memory: residuals in DRAM, predictor in SRAM
idea: Reverse the roles of data and model: a small predictor (e.g. a linear map from layer L-1 KV to layer L KV, or a neighbor-line delta model) lives in on-chip SRAM, and DRAM stores only the quantized residual between prediction and truth; the controller adds prediction and residual back together on read.
why: KV caches and embedding tables are strongly correlated across layers and neighbors, so residuals need 2-4 bits instead of 16: ~3-5x effective capacity on the largest AI memory consumers.

title: Content-addressed physical memory: the hash picks the address
idea: Flip address->content into content->address: the controller hashes each 64 B line and stores it in a slot chosen by the hash, with a reference count; page tables map virtual lines to content IDs, so identical lines (zeros, shared libraries, the same weights across tenants) physically exist once.
why: Line-granular dedup with no software scanning; multi-tenant cloud and VM hosts typically gain 1.3-2x effective capacity.

title: Flash serves reads, DRAM only absorbs writes in inference
idea: Reverse the tier order for read-only data: model weights stream on a fixed layer schedule (so they can be prefetched perfectly) from a many-channel high-bandwidth NAND stack straight into accelerator SRAM, and DRAM/HBM is kept only for the mutable KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are often 50-80% of inference HBM; taking them out of DRAM cuts DRAM bits per served model 2-4x and sidesteps the HBM TSV tax (fact 6).

title: Layer-major batching: one layer resident across thousands of requests
idea: Swap the serving loop nest from token-outer/layer-inner to layer-outer/request-inner: run layer L for a whole queue of thousands of requests, then evict it and load L+1 from flash or far memory, so DRAM holds only one layer's weights plus that layer's KV slice at a time.
why: For throughput-oriented offline inference, resident weights drop by the depth factor (~60-120x) and total DRAM need falls 5-20x, at the cost of latency.

title: Per-block local losses discard activations before next block runs
idea: Reverse the training order from forward-all-then-backward-all to forward-and-learn per block: each block gets an auxiliary head or a forward-gradient estimate, updates at once, and frees its activations before the next block executes.
why: Stored activations are often 60-80% of training memory; per-block learning makes them O(1 block) instead of O(depth), a 10-50x cut in activation memory if accuracy holds.

title: Client-held KV cookies make chat servers stateless between turns
idea: Reverse who stores the conversation: after each turn the server compresses the session KV into a learned latent (~100-500 KB), encrypts and authenticates it, and returns it to the client like an HTTP cookie; the next request uploads it and the server expands it again.
why: Most chat KV sits idle while users read and type; dropping all idle-session state from server DRAM/HBM cuts KV memory 3-10x in consumer services.

title: Compile long shared contexts into adapters instead of KV
idea: Reverse context->weights: documents reused across many requests (codebases, manuals, policies) are distilled offline into a small LoRA or a trained KV 'cartridge' of a few MB, so requests stop holding a 100k-token KV cache for the same text.
why: KV for repeated long contexts drops 10-100x: a few MB of cartridge instead of GBs of KV per concurrent request.

title: Seed-generated tensors regenerate on read instead of being stored
idea: Replace stored pseudo-random structures (random projections, LoRA bases, hashed embedding tables, init-derived weight parts) with a PRNG seed plus a few learned coefficients; an on-chip counter-based generator (Philox-style) recreates each tile at read time.
why: Storage turns into compute: 10-100x smaller footprint for the parts of models and recommenders that can be regenerated, and no DRAM traffic for them.

title: Bit-plane layout: MSB planes in DRAM, LSB planes in flash
idea: Rearrange tensors from word-major to bit-plane-major: the top 3-4 bit planes stay in DRAM and the lower planes live in flash or CXL memory, fetched only when a per-layer confidence monitor (e.g. logit margin) asks for more precision.
why: Most inference steps need only the MSB planes: ~2x effective DRAM capacity and bandwidth for weights and activations, with precision added on demand.

title: Compression pays for ECC: eight-chip DIMMs keep full protection
idea: Reverse 'ECC needs spare chips': the controller compresses each 64 B line by at least 8 bytes (most lines allow it) and writes the ECC into the freed space; the rare incompressible line goes to a small overflow region marked by a pointer flag.
why: Removes the two extra chips in each 10-chip DDR5 RDIMM rank: ~20% fewer DRAM bits bought for server-class reliability.

title: Erasure-coded in-memory shards replace triple DRAM replicas
idea: Instead of keeping 2-3 full DRAM replicas of hot data in in-memory databases and caches, split each object into k data plus m parity shards across nodes (e.g. 10+4 Reed-Solomon) and rebuild over RDMA when a node fails.
why: Resilience overhead drops from 2-3x to ~1.4x of the dataset: 40-55% less DRAM for replicated in-memory tiers.

title: Threads migrate to data so each cluster byte exists once
idea: Reverse data-to-compute: for read-mostly shared sets (embedding tables, graphs) each node holds a disjoint shard, and lightweight threads or continuations hop to the node that owns the next address (Emu-style migration) instead of every node caching replicas.
why: Removes N-fold replicas in clusters: 2-8x less total DRAM for recommendation and graph workloads.

title: Free-before-allocate runtimes shrink garbage-collected heap headroom
idea: Reverse GC's allocate-then-find-garbage order: compiler region inference and escape analysis free most objects deterministically at scope exit, and a forwarding table in the memory controller lets the remaining collector compact concurrently, so heaps run at ~1.2x live data instead of 2-3x.
why: Java, Go and .NET fleets hold a large share of datacenter DRAM; cutting heap headroom 30-50% translates directly into fewer DIMMs.

title: Rack-wide deduplicated page cache in one pooled memory box
idea: Move the OS file page cache, which often fills 30-50% of server DRAM with the same container layers, binaries and datasets, out of every host into one rack-level CXL memory pool indexed by file-content hash; hosts map those pages read-only.
why: One copy per rack instead of one per host: 20-40% less DRAM per server in container-heavy fleets.

title: I/O lands in SRAM, bypassing DRAM bounce buffers entirely
idea: Reverse the I/O path: NICs and SSDs DMA straight into reserved LLC or accelerator SRAM slices under credit-based flow control, and consumers process the data there, so read-once network and storage payloads never stage in DRAM buffers or the page cache.
why: Frees the DRAM held for I/O buffers and staging (10-30% of storage and network appliance memory) and skips the DRAM round trip's 10-20 pJ/bit (fact 5).

title: Speculative pre-free with lineage recompute on surprise reuse
idea: Invert keep-until-proven-dead: the runtime predicts each large object's last use, frees it at once, and keeps only its lineage (the operator and inputs that made it); a mispredicted later read triggers recomputation instead of a fault.
why: Peak memory of dataflow, ML and analytics pipelines drops 20-40% at a bounded recompute cost.

title: Resident key sketches, full KV parked in flash
idea: Flip which part of attention lives in DRAM: only 1-bit sign sketches of the keys plus a graph ANN index stay resident, while full-precision K/V blocks live on NVMe; each decode step fetches only the top-k blocks the sketch picks.
why: Million-token contexts fit in ~1/16-1/32 of the KV DRAM, with the bulk on flash at ~10x lower cost per bit.

title: Attention computed inside SSD controllers, only outputs returned
idea: Reverse data-to-compute for KV: the host sends the query vector to computational SSDs whose controllers run dot-products and softmax-weighted sums over KV stored in NAND, returning only the partial output vector and its normalizer.
why: KV never enters DRAM: KV capacity moves to NAND at ~1/10 the cost per bit, and PCIe traffic per step falls from GBs to KBs.

title: Tenants rent idle DRAM back to the provider every second
idea: Reverse ownership inside each server: VMs and containers hold memory as one-second leases priced by an auction in the hypervisor; tenants earn credits for memory they release, and the host hands it to memory-hungry neighbors through free-page reporting.
why: Cloud servers strand ~25% of DRAM; a market that pays tenants to release it can recover most of that, cutting fleet DRAM purchases 15-25%.

title: Expert-major MoE serving: tokens queue, experts load once per wave
idea: Rearrange MoE serving from token-major to expert-major: tokens routed to cold experts wait in per-expert queues, and each expert's weights stream from flash once per wave to process its whole queue, so only hot experts stay in DRAM.
why: Most experts sit idle at any instant; resident expert weights shrink 3-8x for a bounded rise in latency.

title: Execute directly on compressed data, never decompress into DRAM
idea: Reverse decompress-then-compute: near-memory ALUs run filters, joins and aggregates directly on dictionary-, run-length- and bit-packed column encodings, and LLM kernels consume codebook-quantized weights as indices, so no decompressed copy is ever materialized in DRAM.
why: Removes transient decompressed buffers and keeps data at 3-10x compression throughout analytics and inference.

title: Swap roles: GPU does matmul, CPU DDR hosts attention
idea: Rearrange the accelerator split: the GPU keeps only the weights and runs the dense GEMMs, while the KV cache and the memory-bound attention move to CPU-side DDR5 with CPU or near-memory attention kernels, exchanging small per-token vectors.
why: HBM costs ~3x the wafer area per bit of DDR5 (fact 6); moving KV (often >50% of serving memory) to DDR cuts DRAM wafer area per served token ~2x.

title: Reject-bin DRAM becomes the approximate-data memory tier
idea: Reverse the quality order: dies and DIMMs that fail retention or weak-cell binning (already made, normally scrapped) are packaged into an 'approximate' CXL tier with masked-error semantics, holding error-tolerant data such as video frames, NN activations and low-attention KV.
why: Adds usable bits from yield loss with zero new wafer starts, so no neon excimer litho or helium-cooled etch is used; recovering 3-5% of industry yield loss adds supply on the order of a mid-size fab line.

title: Memory-first chassis: DIMMs outlive three CPU generations
idea: Reverse which part is disposable: servers are built around a 10-year memory backplane (CXL-attached DIMM sleds), and the CPU and accelerator boards become the modules swapped every 3 years, so DRAM is never retired along with the server.
why: Fleet DRAM purchases fall roughly 2-3x over a decade, and the reused bits need no new neon-litho or helium-dependent wafers.

title: HBM stealing: idle neighbor GPUs host overflow KV blocks
idea: Reverse the swap direction from down-to-host to sideways-to-peers: a cluster daemon tracks free HBM on each GPU and pages KV blocks into idle neighbors over NVLink/ICI, ~10x faster than host DDR, before any new memory is bought.
why: GPU fleets often leave 20-40% of HBM unused on some devices; pooling it raises usable capacity by that margin in software alone, with no gas-consuming fabrication.

title: Typing-triggered KV rebuild: drop idle KV, recompute from tokens
idea: Reverse store-versus-recompute for cold sessions: after ~30 s idle, a session's KV is freed and only its token IDs (a few KB) are kept; when the client reports the user is typing, a compute-bound prefill rebuilds the KV on spare tensor cores before the message arrives.
why: Turns idle KV (most of chat KV) into kilobytes: 3-10x less KV memory on installed GPUs, using compute instead of new DRAM made with neon and helium.

title: Model-emitted page-out tokens let the model page its KV
idea: Reverse who manages the cache: fine-tune the model to emit special <page-out span> and <page-in topic> tokens, so it moves the KV of finished sub-tasks to host storage and recalls it itself, like a program managing its own overlays.
why: Long agentic sessions keep only their working set resident: 3-10x less KV in HBM with software on existing hardware, so no new neon- or helium-dependent fab output is needed.

title: Delay-and-cluster scheduler groups requests by shared prefix
idea: Rearrange time: the router holds incoming requests for up to ~150 ms on purpose and releases them in batches grouped by system-prompt or document prefix to the same replica, so one prefix KV copy serves dozens of concurrent requests.
why: Prefix KV duplication across replicas disappears; KV memory per request falls 2-5x for templated workloads, using only scheduling software on installed GPUs.

title: Mesh merging: two half-empty heap pages share one frame
idea: Break the one-virtual-page-per-frame rule: a malloc runtime randomizes object placement so sparse pages rarely collide, finds page pairs whose live objects don't overlap, and remaps both virtual pages onto one physical frame.
why: Compacts fragmented C/C++ heaps 15-40% without moving pointers, in software on existing DRAM; no rare-gas fab steps for new bits.

title: PGO reorders struct fields fleet-wide to delete padding
idea: Rearrange fields literally: a link-time pass uses profiles to reorder struct members by size and co-access, move cold fields into side tables and rewrite every access, applied automatically across a fleet's C, C++ and Rust builds.
why: Padding and cold fields often waste 5-15% of heap bytes; a recompile reclaims them with zero new silicon, so no neon or helium fab steps.

title: Permute weight channels so neighbors compress, then delta-code
idea: Rearrange the order of rows and channels inside each weight matrix (with the matching permutation folded into the next layer) so similar channels sit side by side, then store each channel as a low-bit delta from its predecessor.
why: Adds ~1.3-2x near-lossless compression on top of quantization for weights held in existing DRAM; the permutation is free at runtime and needs no new hardware.

title: Follow-the-sun memory: batch work chases idle DRAM across continents
idea: Rearrange workloads in time and space: batch inference, embedding generation and analytics move every few hours to regions whose interactive demand is in its nightly trough, so each region's DRAM is sized for a flattened global load instead of its local peak.
why: Peak-to-average DRAM provisioning of ~1.6-2x shrinks toward ~1.2x, so 20-35% fewer DIMMs are bought; pure orchestration with no neon or helium.

title: Certify crypto-erase so retired DIMMs are resold, not shredded
idea: Reverse the security default: a NIST/ISO-certified power-off and pattern-overwrite attestation for volatile DRAM, with signed logs from the server BMC, replaces mandatory physical shredding of memory modules in government and enterprise disposal rules.
why: DRAM is volatile, yet shredding destroys working capacity that could supply the secondary market; every reused GB replaces new fab output that would need neon litho and helium-cooled tools.

title: Mercury-lamp i-line compression chips tiled on every DIMM
idea: Move memory compression from the CPU to the memory: many slow, wide BDI/LZ compressor lanes are built in 350 nm i-line fabs (mercury arc lamps instead of neon excimer lasers, argon-free fluorine etch with N2 diluent) and tiled on the DIMM or CXL card, each lane handling a slice of bank traffic.
why: ~2x effective capacity per DIMM, with the helper silicon coming from depreciated, gas-light U.S. fabs instead of EUV/ArF lines.

title: Cache becomes main memory: DRAM-less servers for small-state services
idea: Reverse the hierarchy: services whose working set fits in large stacked caches (DNS, firewalls, routing, rate limiters, lookup services under ~256 MB across sockets) are rewritten to run entirely from 3D-stacked L3/SRAM with flash as backing, and their servers ship with one minimal DIMM or none.
why: Removes tens to hundreds of GB of DRAM per such node using CPU SKUs already in production, so no new DRAM bits and no rare-gas fab demand.

title: Snapshot-and-restore replaces warm serverless sandbox pools
idea: Reverse 'keep warm' into 'keep cold, restore fast': idle function sandboxes are snapshotted to NVMe and restored in ~5-10 ms by lazily faulting in only the pages the first invocation touches, instead of holding thousands of warm VMs in DRAM.
why: Warm pools often leave 50-80% of serverless DRAM idle; replacing them cuts that DRAM 3-5x in software alone.

title: Admit LLM requests by predicted KV-seconds, not arrival order
idea: Reverse the scheduler's input: a small regressor predicts each request's output length and context so the scheduler admits and orders work by predicted KV-byte-seconds (shortest-KV-first, with preemption) instead of FIFO, bounding peak KV rather than provisioning for it.
why: Peak KV memory falls ~1.5-2x at equal throughput, delivered as a software update on installed accelerators.

title: Fuse the optimizer into backward so gradients never fully exist
idea: Rearrange the training step from backward-then-update to update-during-backward: the optimizer applies each parameter tensor's gradient the moment it is produced and frees it at once, with gradient clipping taken from a running norm of the previous step.
why: Removes the full gradient buffer (the size of the model): 25-40% lower training memory on existing GPUs, with no new gas-dependent DRAM output.

title: Shared inverted page tables end per-process mapping copies
idea: Reverse the page-table direction for shared memory: one table per shared physical region (indexed by frame, or a kernel-shared upper-level table) is linked into every process that maps it, instead of each of hundreds of database worker processes building its own copy.
why: Databases with large shared buffers can burn tens of GB on duplicate page tables; sharing them recovers that DRAM with a kernel change alone.

title: Guests drop their page cache so one host cache serves all
idea: Reverse double caching in virtualization: guest kernels mount files through DAX over virtio-pmem/virtiofs, so file pages come straight from the host's single page cache, and guests report free pages back at once.
why: Removes the duplicate guest-plus-host cache layers, often 20-30% of VM-host DRAM, with software on today's hypervisors and no new silicon that needs rare gases.

title: Harvest laptop and console DRAM from e-waste into CXL sleds
idea: Reverse the supply chain: automated desolder, reball and burn-in lines pull DDR4/DDR5 BGA packages from recycled laptops, consoles and SO-DIMMs, bin them by speed and retention, and remount them on CXL far-memory cards behind a compression controller.
why: E-waste holds large amounts of DRAM that is already made; reclaiming it adds U.S.-processed memory supply with no neon litho or helium use.

title: 32-bit relative pointers ABI shrinks C/C++ heaps
idea: Reverse the 64-bit default: an allocator ABI puts each process's heap in 4 GB regions and the compiler stores pointers as 32-bit offsets from a region base register (as Java compressed oops and V8 already do), using fat pointers only where regions are crossed.
why: Pointer-heavy data structures shrink 25-40%, recovering DRAM through a recompile of software on existing CPUs.

title: Fleet DIMM gleaning: telemetry-guided physical rebalancing of installed memory
idea: Rearrange the DIMMs already installed across a fleet: per-server memory telemetry finds hosts whose peak use never exceeds half their DRAM, and technicians pull those modules during routine maintenance and install them in memory-starved hosts of the same generation.
why: Fleets often have 20-30% of DRAM never touched; moving it costs far less than buying new bits at 4x prices and needs no rare gases.

title: Frequency-domain KV: DCT along sequence, drop high bands
idea: Rearrange the KV cache from time order to frequency order: blocks of 64 tokens are transformed per channel with a DCT along the sequence axis, high-frequency coefficients are quantized hard or dropped, and attention reads the inverse-transformed block.
why: KV channels change slowly across neighboring tokens, so 3-6x compression beyond token quantization is plausible, as a kernel on existing GPUs with no new silicon.

title: Idle consumer PCs and consoles run offline batch AI jobs
idea: Reverse where batch AI lives: embedding generation, evaluation sweeps and synthetic-data jobs are split into small-model shards and dispatched (Folding@home-style, for paid credits) to idle gaming PCs and consoles whose 16-32 GB of DRAM and GPUs sit unused most hours.
why: Shifts latency-tolerant memory demand off datacenter DRAM onto hundreds of millions of GB already built; no new fab output, so no neon or helium.
